title: The 5 Practices
subtitle: The routine that turns a rich task into real learning — how a teacher orchestrates a productive discussion instead of hoping one happens.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Smith & Stein, 5 Practices for Orchestrating Productive Mathematics Discussions (2011) · NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014).

blocks.text: Five deliberate moves — **Anticipate, Monitor, Select, Sequence, Connect** — that a teacher uses to run a task-based lesson so that student thinking adds up to the intended mathematics (Smith & Stein, 2011).

Without them, a rich task becomes “share out” roulette: the teacher asks “who wants to show their work?”, takes volunteers in random order, and hopes the math lands. The 5 Practices replace luck with intention — the teacher decides in advance what to look for, watches for it, and builds the consolidation from chosen student work in a planned order.

Rich Tasks, Thin-Slicing, and three-act math all depend on this. The task creates the thinking; the 5 Practices are how the teacher harvests that thinking into formal mathematics. It is the single most important facilitation skill in Core Instruction — and it is the grown-up version of the recording-and-connecting teachers rehearsed in Number Talks.

rows: Do the task yourself; predict the strategies and misconceptions students will produce, and how you’ll respond to each.
Circulate, watch, and note who is doing what. Ask purposeful questions; resist rescuing.
Choose *specific* student work to make public — not volunteers, but the pieces that build the story.
Decide the order to present them — usually accessible/concrete → abstract — so the discussion builds.
Make the links explicit: between strategies, to the representations, and to the formal math and the goal.

blocks.text: The first move happens at the planning table (often in a PLC); the last four happen live, in the lesson.

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: The teacher circulating with a purpose, noting strategies
Student work shared in a deliberate order, not random volunteers
“How is Maria’s way connected to Devon’s?”
The formal mathematics named at the end, anchored in student work
A planning sheet with anticipated strategies

no.title: We should not see
items: “Who wants to share?” with no plan
Only the fastest/most confident students presenting
Disconnected show-and-tell with no synthesis
The teacher re-teaching their own method instead of using student work
The task ending with no consolidation

blocks.title: The move teachers skip — and shouldn’t

blocks.text: **Anticipate.** It’s invisible (it happens before class) so it’s the first to get dropped, and without it the other four collapse — you can’t select and sequence strategies you didn’t predict. Anticipating *is* the PLC “do the math first” habit. Protect it.

items: **Selecting on purpose** (not by raised hands) lets you feature the thinking of students who rarely volunteer — a direct lever for distributing status.
**Sequencing from accessible to sophisticated** means more students see an approach they understand early, before the harder ones.
**Monitoring** tells you who needs access support *now*, in the moment, rather than discovering it on a test later.

sections.label: Lesson design connection

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson
The 5 Practices wrap around a **rich task** — one move before the lesson, four during. They are not a separate activity; they are *how you run the task*.
Practice 1 — Anticipate (in the PLC, before class)
Solve the task yourself, then build an **anticipation guide**:

headers: Where it fits in the consolidation
rows: “What pattern do you notice in the table?”
“How does your picture show the rate?”
“Where do the table values live in your equation?”
“Does doubling the input double the output here?”

items: **Monitor.** Circulate with your anticipation guide. Check off strategies as you see them; jot names. Ask the questions you planned. *Don’t rescue* — ask, then step back.
**Select.** From what you saw, choose 3–4 pieces of student work that build the mathematical story (not the four fastest finishers).
**Sequence.** Order them deliberately — usually concrete/accessible first, the formal/efficient one last, with a misconception placed where it teaches the most.

**Connect.** In the consolidation, draw the explicit links: “How is the table related to the equation? Why do these two strategies get the same answer?” Name the formal mathematics and tie it back to the learning goal.

blocks.text: A clipboard grid: rows = anticipated strategies, columns = blank for student names. As you circulate, write a name in the row that matches what you see. By the time you stop the task, your grid already tells you *who* to call on and *in what order* — Select and Sequence are half-done.

items: **Name the math goal** the task serves — the connect at the end aims here.
**Anticipate** in your PLC (do the math; list strategies & misconceptions).
**Build the monitoring grid** from your anticipated strategies.
**Decide your likely sequence** in advance (you’ll adjust live based on what students actually do).
**Protect time for Connect** — if you run out of time before consolidating, the task did not teach.

blocks.text: Teachers who built Number Talks already know how to record strategies and ask “how are these alike?” — that’s Monitoring and Connecting in miniature. The 5 Practices simply scale those moves from one mental-math problem to a full task. This is why the openers came first.

items: **Use Select to lift status:** deliberately feature a strong idea from a student who rarely shares (“watch what this group noticed”).
**Sequence for access:** lead with the representation most students can follow, so no one is lost before the formal version.
**Monitor for access, not just answers:** note who is stuck on *language or the task* versus the mathematics, and scaffold accordingly.

blocks.text: Once the 5 Practices are routine, every rich task, thin-sliced sequence, and three-act lesson lands reliably — because the teacher always knows how to turn what students did into the mathematics they were meant to learn. It is the connective tissue of the entire Core.
